title: Regular Expressions for Operations
intro:
Log lines, alert rules, routing rules, and validation checks are all written in regular expressions, and a slightly wrong one fails quietly: it matches too much or nothing. This tutorial uses grep and sed on app.log, whose lines look like:
2026-09-28T12:00:01Z level=ERROR user=dana ip=203.0.113.9 status=502 duration=1904ms msg="upstream timeout"

steps.prompt: Show the lines whose level is ERROR or FATAL, using extended regular expressions.
steps.fake_output:
2026-09-28T12:00:01Z level=ERROR user=dana ip=203.0.113.9 status=502 duration=1904ms msg="upstream timeout"
2026-09-28T12:00:07Z level=FATAL user=sam ip=198.51.100.14 status=500 duration=12ms msg="out of memory"
steps.why: -E turns on extended syntax, where | means 'or' and parentheses group without backslashes. Including 'level=' in the pattern matters: searching for just ERROR would also match a message that happens to contain the word. Make a pattern as specific as the thing you mean.

steps.prompt: Extract just the IP addresses from the file, one per line, not the whole lines.
steps.explanation: Only the matched text: one to three digits, then three more groups of a dot and digits.
steps.why: -o prints the match alone, which turns grep into an extraction tool; pipe it into 'sort | uniq -c' for counts. The dot is escaped because an unescaped '.' matches any character, so '1.2.3.4' as a pattern also matches '1x2y3z4'. Forgetting that is the most common regex bug in alert and routing rules.

steps.prompt: Pull out the status codes with sed: print only the number after status= from each line.
steps.explanation: The captured digits, one per line.
steps.why: Parentheses capture, and \1 is what the first pair captured. The pattern matches the whole line and replaces it with just the capture; -n with the trailing p prints only lines where the substitution happened. This capture-and-replace shape is the same in Prometheus relabelling rules, Loki queries, and log-shipper configs.

steps.prompt: Before sharing the log, hide the user names: replace every user=<name> with user=REDACTED, printing the result.
steps.fake_output:
2026-09-28T12:00:01Z level=ERROR user=REDACTED ip=203.0.113.9 status=502 duration=1904ms msg="upstream timeout"
2026-09-28T12:00:07Z level=FATAL user=REDACTED ip=198.51.100.14 status=500 duration=12ms msg="out of memory"
steps.explanation: Each user value replaced, everything else untouched.
steps.why: '[^ ]+' means 'one or more characters that aren't a space', which stops at the end of the value. That's the safe way to say 'up to the next delimiter'. The tempting alternative, 'user=.*', leads to the next step.

steps.prompt:
Someone wrote the redaction as  s/user=.* /user=REDACTED /  instead. What does it do to a line?
  a) The same thing
  b) It replaces everything from user= up to the LAST space on the line, deleting the ip, status, and duration fields too
  c) Nothing
  d) It only matches the first character
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
input : ... level=ERROR user=dana ip=203.0.113.9 status=502 duration=1904ms msg="upstream timeout"
output: ... level=ERROR user=REDACTED timeout"
steps.hint: '.*' takes as much as it can.
steps.explanation: Greedy matching: '.*' runs to the last possible space, swallowing most of the line.
steps.why: Quantifiers are greedy: they match as much as possible and give back only what they must. The fixes are a negated class ('[^ ]+'), or a lazy quantifier ('.*?') in engines that have one; grep -E and sed don't, grep -P and most programming languages do. Greedy '.*' in the middle of a pattern is the usual cause of both wrong matches and very slow ones. Test a regex against lines that should NOT match as well as ones that should.
